title: From Characters to Integers: nanoGPT's Shakespeare Prep
objective: Follow the code in data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py:23-45 as it builds a character vocabulary from the text, maps each character to an integer and back, splits the raw text 90/10 into train and validation, and then encodes both splits into integer ids.
audience_context: The learner has this code span open (data/shakespeare_char/prepare.py lines 23-45 in nanoGPT) and asked for a 60-second explanation of it. The raw text is already loaded into `data` before this span begins.
scope_note: Covers only lines 23-45 as given. Loading or downloading the text before this span, and anything after the train token-count print (such as saving the ids or metadata), are left out because the excerpt doesn't show them.

evidence.excerpt:
# get all the unique characters that occur in this text
chars = sorted(list(set(data)))
vocab_size = len(chars)
print("all the unique characters:", ''.join(chars))
print(f"vocab size: {vocab_size:,}")

# create a mapping from characters to integers
stoi = { ch:i for i,ch in enumerate(chars) }
itos = { i:ch for i,ch in enumerate(chars) }
def encode(s):
    return [stoi[c] for c in s] # encoder: take a string, output a list of integers
def decode(l):
    return ''.join([itos[i] for i in l]) # decoder: take a list of integers, output a string

# create the train and test splits
n = len(data)
train_data = data[:int(n*0.9)]
val_data = data[int(n*0.9):]

# encode both to integers
train_ids = encode(train_data)
val_ids = encode(val_data)
print(f"train has {len(train_ids):,} tokens")

claim_registry.text: `chars = sorted(list(set(data)))` collects every unique character in the whole text `data` and sorts them, and `vocab_size = len(chars)` is the number of those unique characters.
`stoi = { ch:i for i,ch in enumerate(chars) }` gives each character its position in the sorted `chars` list as its integer id, and `itos` is the reverse mapping from integer back to character.
`encode(s)` turns a string into a list of integers, one per character, using `stoi`. `decode(l)` turns a list of integers back into a string using `itos` and `''.join`.

The raw text is split by position: `train_data = data[:int(n*0.9)]` takes the first 90% of the characters and `val_data = data[int(n*0.9):]` takes the remaining 10%. Each split is one contiguous slice, not a random sample.

Only after the split are both parts encoded: `train_ids = encode(train_data)` and `val_ids = encode(val_data)`. Each character becomes exactly one token, so the token count printed for train equals its character count.

must_show: The line `chars = sorted(list(set(data)))`, with a short illustrative text dropping its duplicate characters and the remaining unique characters lining up in sorted order
`vocab_size` shown as the count of that sorted character row
A two-way lookup table built from the sorted row: characters with their index numbers (`stoi`) and the same pairs read from number to character (`itos`)
`encode` turning a short string into a list of integers one character at a time, and `decode` turning that list back into the same string
The full text as one long strip cut at the 90% mark into `train_data` (first, larger part) and `val_data` (last 10%)
Both slices then passing through `encode` to become `train_ids` and `val_ids`
The matching code line highlighted at each step, moving down the span from line 23 to line 45
must_not_claim: The vocabulary is built from the training split only
Integer ids are assigned by how often a character appears or by the order it first appears in the text
The train/validation split shuffles or randomly samples characters
The text is encoded first and then the integer list is split
encode merges several characters into one token or compresses the text, as subword tokenizers do
decode loses information or cannot rebuild the original string
This code span writes the encoded ids to files
